bib.title: Before you model: Communication and logistics of projects (Chapter 4, Machine Learning Engineering in Action)
authors: Ben Wilson (per caller; chapter PDF does not print author)
bib.venue: Manning (book chapter; publisher and year not printed in the chapter PDF)

question: How should an ML team communicate, schedule reviews, limit experimentation and plan business rules before and during modeling so that a project reaches production?
contributions: Time limits and maintainability questions for experimentation
Taxonomy of development anti-patterns: PDD, CDD, RDD
Business rules chaos planning, human-in-the-loop, fallbacks

results.claim: Projects that never reach production share one consistent theme: a lack of communication, above all between the DS team and the requesting business unit.
results.setup: Author's experience building ML recommendation-engine style projects; no data presented
results.where: p.81 sidebar 'What we have here is a failure to communicate'

results.claim: The first planning meeting should ask why, what, how-done-now, ideal solution and willingness-to-pay questions, and focus on what to build and why rather than how.
results.setup: Author's experience building ML recommendation-engine style projects; no data presented

results.claim: Hold milestone-driven meetings with tangible results to review, not fixed-cadence meetings: experimental update, SME/prototype review, development progress reviews, MVP review with UAT, preproduction review.
results.setup: Author's experience building ML recommendation-engine style projects; no data presented

results.claim: Experimentation should be time-boxed and minimal (basic tuning, small demo set, rough implicit weights), and the experimental code is throwaway and should not be extended into the final solution.
results.setup: Author's experience building ML recommendation-engine style projects; no data presented

results.claim: Choose the prototype by maintainability, cost to retrain, team skill, testability, auditability and extensibility, not only best results.
results.setup: Author's experience building ML recommendation-engine style projects; no data presented

results.claim: Business rules (contract requirements, offense filters) must be identified early, built as configurable levers rather than hardcoded values, and be modifiable by SMEs under validation controls; add a fallback for sparse or missing data.
results.setup: Author's experience building ML recommendation-engine style projects; no data presented

results.claim: A rule-of-thumb for RDD detection: feature engineering code to model code ratio should exceed 4x.
results.unit: ratio of feature-engineering code to model code
results.setup: Author's rule of thumb for 'the vast majority of ML solutions'; no supporting data
results.quote: to model code should always be > 4x.

results.claim: UAT scores should be normalised per reviewer and raters must not be vested in the project; unanimous praise is a warning sign of creator bias.
results.setup: Author's experience building ML recommendation-engine style projects; no data presented

results.claim: Preproduction readiness described in the worked scenario: load test at 10 times peak user volume and a week or more of stable running in a stress environment.
results.setup: Illustrative recommendation-engine release scenario, not a measured result
results.quote: responsiveness measured through simulation of 10 times the user volume at peak traf

limits: All claims come from the author's personal experience; no data, surveys or measurements are presented.
Worked example is a single e-commerce recommendation engine (ALS, collaborative filtering, FP-growth); dates and team sizes in figures are illustrative.
Assumes a company over 1,000 employees with separate DE, frontend and product teams; the chapter says smaller companies fold roles together.
Predates LLM-era systems; no evaluation, monitoring or drift content.
practices: Open the first planning meeting with why, what, how-done-now, ideal solution and willingness-to-pay questions; keep discussion on what to build (p.78-79, Fig 4.1).
Always build the simplest solution possible to solve the problem (p.79).
Draw a user-journey or flow-path wireframe to engage non-technical members; keep architecture and model debates inside the DS team (p.82-85).
Record nice-to-have ideas with a stated cost rather than discarding them, and keep the MVP to essentials (p.85).
Assign a time-available SME with authority as project champion, not the executive sponsor (p.89).
Schedule meetings at project milestones, not on a weekly cadence; eliminate pure status meetings (p.89-95).
Be honest about delivery dates; do not under-promise to pad schedules (p.92).
Experimental update meeting asks only 'can we actually figure this out?': progress, risks, solvability (p.102).
Demo with real data from the SMEs' own accounts and record negative impressions (p.104).
If unsure, answer 'I don't know, but I'll go find out' (p.104).
Show fixes using the same data that exposed the problem; do not just claim the feature is checked in (p.105).
Do not silently 'ninja-solve' blockers; notify only the teams affected, and the full team for business-critical issues (p.106).

After MVP, spend sprints on code hardening before release; run UAT with reviewers not invested in the project, normalise scores per reviewer, bring in outsiders if feedback is all positive (p.106-107).
Preproduction review asks 'did we build what we set out to build?', walks the original features in QA, and sets up self-service A/B metrics datasets; never release on a Friday (p.100, 108).
Tell stakeholders to wait for statistically valid data before judging results (p.100-101).
Time-box experimentation, test the minimum needed to pick an approach, and keep experimental code throwaway (p.109-111).
Ask maintainability, cost-to-retrain, skill, testability, auditability and extensibility questions before choosing the prototype (p.112).
Blend TDD testability with FDD feature focus, scaled to project complexity (p.113-114).
Test more than one model and framework; a single option with no prior experience signals prayer-driven development (p.115).
Do not skip experimentation (chaos-driven development) and avoid overengineered show-off designs (resume-driven development) (p.115-116).
Plan business rules as levers and knobs via passed-in configuration, never hardcoded; classify them as required Business Rules versus testable Business Assumptions (p.117-119).
Let SMEs modify rules without downtime but under validation controls (p.119).
Provide a fallback (e.g. global popularity) for cold-start or missing data (p.119-120).
Explain ML limits via the realms-of-data picture; answer 'we don't have the data to answer that' honestly (p.120-122).

terms.definition: a simulation of a product, exploring how a new feature or system will be consumed by a particular user

terms.term: scope creep (ML death by a thousand requests)
terms.definition: requests for additional features that materialise when a demo is shown to a team uninformed of the planning
additional nuances to ML (restrictions and controls) that augment model results, e.g. contractual obligations and offense filters
handing problems one does not know how to solve to some all-knowing person who has solved it before, eliminating proper research and evaluation
skipping experimentation and prototyping phases altogether (cowboy development)
designing an overengineered, show-off implementation to a problem
code tested, system works as a whole on production-scale data, all agreed features complete and performing as designed
user-acceptance testing, measuring subjective quality of the solution by people external to the project
